Abuse of the Market Maker Exemption and T+6 Settlement Loophole 
The execution of naked short sales inevitably leads to settlement failures, formally known as 
Fails to Deliver (FTDs) within the Continuous Net Settlement (CNS) system managed by the 
DTCC.1 Under standard U.S. equity settlement rules applicable during the investigative period, 
securities were required to be delivered by the third business day following the trade date, a 
standard known as T+3.1 
Predictably, Scout Trading systematically failed to deliver the ETF shares by the T+3 deadline 
because they never borrowed them in the first place.1 To avoid the forced buy-ins and severe 
trading restrictions mandated by Regulation SHO for failing to deliver securities, Scout Trading 
falsely relied upon a regulatory loophole designed exclusively for legitimate liquidity providers.1 
Rule 204 of Regulation SHO permits bona fide market makers an extended settlement window 
of T+6 (six days after the trade date) to resolve fails to deliver.1 This exemption exists to 
acknowledge the inherent inventory and liquidity risks faced by market makers who provide 
continuous two-sided quotes to the broader market.1 The regulatory investigation conclusively 
determined that Scout Trading’s activities did not qualify as bona fide market making.1 Bleich’s 
firm was effectively masquerading as a market maker solely to access the T+6 extended 
settlement window.1 This loophole allowed the firm to maintain massive, unhedged, naked 
short positions for six full trading days without incurring a single cent in the exorbitant 
borrowing costs.1 
The execution of the scheme was highly cyclical and automated.1 On the morning of the T+6 
deadline, just before regular trading hours commenced, Scout Trading would finally submit an 
order to establish ETF creation units (or purchase shares on the secondary market), 
momentarily closing out the fail-to-deliver within the CNS system.1 However, on the very next 
trading day (T+7), the firm would immediately submit another naked redemption order or 
execute another open market short sale, effectively resetting the compliance clock and 
re-establishing the short position.1 This continuous loop allowed the firm to maximize the 
duration of its short exposure, perpetually rolling the fails forward and exploiting the structural 
decay of the ETFs for proprietary financial gain.1 
Systemic Market Impact and the Threshold Securities List 
The scale of Scout Trading’s regulatory circumvention was not merely a technical or 
administrative violation; it was vast enough to generate significant systemic risk and 
measurable market distortion that impacted all other market participants.1 
During the investigative period, FINRA determined that Scout Trading submitted at least 255 
naked redemption orders through its clearing firm across eleven of the 14 targeted ETFs.1
